reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Epidermolysis bullosa is a group of inherited disorders in which minor friction or trauma causes blistering and skin fragility, usually presenting at or soon after birth
It is classified by the level of skin cleavage: simplex (within the epidermis), junctional (at the basement membrane zone), dystrophic (below the basement membrane), and Kindler EB (mixed levels)
The plane of splitting predicts scarring: intra-epidermal simplex forms tend to heal without scarring, whereas dystrophic forms scar and can cause fusion of digits (mitten deformity)
Extracutaneous involvement is common in severe subtypes, including oral, oesophageal, ocular, and genitourinary mucosae, leading to feeding difficulty, strictures, and malnutrition
Care is multidisciplinary and centres on meticulous wound care, non-adherent dressings, infection control, pain management, nutrition, and prevention of trauma
Handle affected neonates and children gently, avoiding shearing forces, adhesive tapes, and friction that can strip the skin
Junctional EB includes a severe generalised form with high infant mortality, while severe recessive dystrophic EB carries a substantial lifetime risk of aggressive squamous cell carcinoma
Accurate subtyping through skin biopsy with mapping and genetic testing guides prognosis, genetic counselling, and emerging targeted therapies
reference.pathophysiology: Epidermolysis bullosa results from mutations in genes encoding structural proteins that anchor the layers of skin together. Defects in keratins (such as KRT5 and KRT14) weaken the basal keratinocyte cytoskeleton in simplex forms; defects in laminin-332 and other hemidesmosomal components disrupt adhesion at the basement membrane in junctional forms; and defects in type VII collagen, the main component of anchoring fibrils, undermine attachment of the epidermis to the dermis in dystrophic forms. The specific protein deficiency determines the level at which the skin separates under mechanical stress, the tendency to scar, and the pattern of extracutaneous complications. Repeated blistering, wound healing, and chronic inflammation drive fibrosis and, in severe dystrophic disease, malignant transformation.
additionalDifferentials: Bullous impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Autoimmune blistering diseases (e.g. pemphigoid gestationis affecting the neonate, linear IgA disease)
Incontinentia pigmenti in its vesicular stage
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy for immunofluorescence antigen mapping to identify the level of cleavage
Transmission electron microscopy in specialised centres
Molecular genetic testing to confirm subtype and enable counselling
Nutritional, growth, and haematological monitoring (including for anaemia) in severe disease
Surveillance for oesophageal strictures, dental disease, and, in dystrophic EB, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
redFlags: Extensive blistering and skin loss in a neonate with fluid, electrolyte, and thermoregulatory compromise and high infection risk
Sepsis arising from chronically open wounds
New, non-healing, or indurated ulcer in severe dystrophic EB suggesting aggressive squamous cell carcinoma
Oesophageal stricturing causing dysphagia, malnutrition, and failure to thrive
Airway or ocular involvement compromising breathing or vision
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies enormously by subtype: localised simplex forms are compatible with a near-normal lifespan, whereas severe junctional disease can be fatal in infancy and severe recessive dystrophic disease causes progressive disability, contractures, malnutrition, and a high risk of fatal squamous cell carcinoma in adulthood.
pitfalls: Assuming all EB is mild and underestimating the severity of junctional or dystrophic subtypes
Using adhesive dressings or tapes that strip fragile skin
Neglecting nutrition, pain, and psychological support in chronic disease
Failing to arrange skin cancer surveillance in severe dystrophic EB
Delaying accurate subtyping and genetic counselling that guide management and family planning
management: Deliver meticulous wound care with non-adherent atraumatic dressings, lancing tense blisters to prevent lateral extension while leaving the roof intact
Prevent trauma through gentle handling, protective padding and strict avoidance of adhesive tapes and shearing forces
Practise infection control with topical antiseptics, swab and treat wound infection, and remain alert to sepsis and colonisation delaying healing
Optimise nutrition with high-energy, high-protein intake and iron for anaemia, and dilate or manage oesophageal strictures to maintain feeding
Provide analgesia and antipruritic measures, as pain and itch are major burdens
Undertake surveillance for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in dystrophic subtypes, alongside dental, ophthalmic and growth monitoring
Coordinate a multidisciplinary team of dermatology, specialist nurses, dietitians, dentistry, physiotherapy and psychology
Offer genetic counselling and confirm subtype by antigen mapping and molecular testing, signposting emerging gene and cell therapies
